item.title: Tyler, The Creator’s Sold-Out Camp Flog Gnaw Streams Free Worldwide
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Tyler, The Creator's sold-out Camp Flog Gnaw will stream free worldwide through Amazon Music, Prime Video and Twitch.
item.content:encoded:
Tyler, The Creator‘s sold-out Camp Flog Gnaw Carnival is opening its gates to fans far beyond Los Angeles. Amazon Music confirmed the two-day festival will stream free worldwide when it returns to the Dodger Stadium grounds on November 14 and 15.

The live feed will be available through the Amazon Music app, Prime Video, Twitch and Amazon Live. “No subscription is required,” Amazon said, giving fans several ways to watch the 12th edition without a festival pass.

This is the fourth straight year Amazon Music has carried Camp Flog Gnaw. The company said the 2026 show sold out immediately and includes more than 40 artists across Hip-Hop, R&B, rock and other genres.

Wayno and Jillian Superstar will host the broadcast. Their coverage will include performances, backstage interviews and other pieces from the carnival throughout the weekend.

The live programming is scheduled to begin at 2:45 P.M. Pacific Time on both Saturday and Sunday. That timing gives the broadcast room to carry afternoon sets before the festival’s 11 P.M. local curfew.

Viewers outside the United States will also get another window. Daily international rebroadcasts are set to begin at 8 A.M. GMT on November 15 and 16, after live coverage starts in Los Angeles.

Camp Flog Gnaw has become one of Hip-Hop’s biggest artist-led festivals since Tyler launched it in 2012. Goldenvoice produces the carnival, which mixes full concert sets with rides, games and the visual world Tyler has built around his music and Golf brand.

Previous editions have brought Childish Gambino, SZA, A$AP Rocky, Solange, Doechii, Kaytranada, Lil Yachty, GloRilla, Erykah Badu, André 3000 and Lauryn Hill to the festival. Tyler has remained the centerpiece, using the bill to move freely between rap, R&B, and alternative music.

The official festival schedule lists noon opening times and an 11 p.m. curfew on both days. The event is all ages and will go forward rain or shine.

For fans who could not get into the sold-out grounds, the free stream turns the weekend into a global show. Amazon Music has also posted an official Camp Flog Gnaw playlist ahead of the first performance.

item.title: Vince Staples Explains Why He Avoids Other Music While Writing
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Vince Staples explained why he avoided other artists' music while writing and how daily life shaped the work he made.
item.content:encoded:
Vince Staples said he avoided other artists’ music while writing and turned to his own life.

“I don’t like to be inspired by other music,” he told Harper’s Bazaar. “I feel like it’s a disservice to the lives that we live every day.”

His interview, recorded this summer, accompanied the magazine’s November 3 feature naming him its guest music director. He connected music with the memories it brought back.

His album, Cry Baby, arrived June 5 through his Section Eight Arthouse imprint in partnership with Loma Vista Recordings. The ten-song release followed 2024’s Dark Times.

Loma Vista described the record as “a more outwardly facing artistic statement and piece of social commentary,” following the personal focus of his previous work.

The change reached beyond subject matter. Apple Music’s album notes described a sound built on noise rock and post-punk. Its account of “Go! Go! Gorilla” pointed to Staples recalling a police encounter when he was 12. On “7 In The Morning,” the record dealt with war as entertainment.

His work outside the recording booth had fed back into his music, too. As AllHipHop previously reported, Staples said making “The Vince Staples Show” taught him to run music projects more efficiently. He co-created the Netflix series, starred in it and served as an executive producer.

He also brought those concerns into the room with him when he performed at NPR’s Tiny Desk. The set, released July 21, paired material from Cry Baby with “Shame On The Devil” from Dark Times. Two guitarists, a bassist and a drummer backed him, with all four musicians also credited on background vocals.

The lineup included Jennifer Haack and Mikaiah Lei on guitar, Chloe Haack on bass and Myles Martin on drums. He opened with “Blackberry Marmalade” and closed with “Only In America,” putting the new album at both ends of the performance.

Between songs, Staples asked the audience about Black history. “What about Bobby Hutton?” he asked, after first bringing up George Jackson. NPR’s account of the performance said no one raised a hand. He also named Larry Kimmons, who was killed by a Pepperdine University security guard in 1969.

item.title: Stove God Cooks Locks In Warner Records Partnership
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Stove God Cooks and Babygrande Records join Warner Records for an early-2027 album release backed by Swizz Beatz.
item.content:encoded:
Stove God Cooks is bringing his long-delayed second album to Warner Records through a new partnership with Babygrande Records.

The labels announced that Warner will join Babygrande to release All This For Me?, the Syracuse rapper’s first full-length project since his 2020 debut Reasonable Drought. The album is now expected in early 2027, with Swizz Beatz producing the project and serving as executive producer.

The partnership announcement adds structure to a rollout that has been delayed more than once. Stove God and Babygrande previously aimed to release the album in March. That date passed, leaving fans waiting while the rapper kept working through features and new records.

Stove God said the new deal confirms the direction he chose after a difficult stretch.

“Everything played out exactly how it was supposed to. Real power is knowing when to walk away! Even from something the world thinks you need,” said Stove God Cooks. “A lot of people are afraid to do that. I’m not one of them. When God has His hand on you, what’s meant for you can’t miss you. This new season isn’t luck! It’s confirmation! I’m excited about this next chapter and what we’re building with Warner Records, but even more excited to give my fans the music and the moment they’ve patiently waited for.”

Babygrande founder and CEO Chuck Wilson said the Warner connection grew out of a relationship with Julian Petty, Warner Records’ executive vice president and head of business and legal affairs. Wilson said he had sent Petty updates about Stove God over the years before the two sides met in Los Angeles.

“Relationships are everything in the music business,” Wilson said.

Petty also has history with Babygrande. He described the arrangement as a chance to work again with a former legal client while helping Stove God reach a wider audience.

The partnership arrives as the rapper restarts the album campaign with “STOVIE’S HOME (Down Down).” The Swizz Beatz-produced single opened a fresh chapter for an album that has been discussed for years.

Stove God built his reputation through Reasonable Drought, produced entirely by Roc Marciano, and a run of scene-stealing appearances with Westside Gunn and other Griselda artists. His verse and hook on Clipse’s “F.I.C.O.” added another high-profile moment to that run.

Warner and Babygrande did not announce an exact release date for All This For Me?. The early-2027 window gives the partners time to turn the renewed single campaign into the album launch Stove God’s listeners have been waiting for. It also gives Warner a clear role in extending the record’s reach beyond the underground audience that kept the demand alive.

item.title: Dawn Richard Calls Diddy-Dirty Money Work Environment “Volatile”
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Dawn Richard says control inside Diddy-Dirty Money created a volatile workplace while she was expected to stay grateful.
item.content:encoded:
Dawn Richard described her time in Diddy-Dirty Money as “volatile” and said the group’s work environment “wasn’t normal” during a new sitdown with television producer Carlos King.

The singer revisited that chapter of her career in a November 4 conversation on King’s Reality with the King platform.

Her account adds another first-person description of life inside Sean “Diddy” Combs’ Bad Boy system, years after Richard moved from Danity Kane into Diddy-Dirty Money.

Richard, Kalenna Harper and Combs made up the trio, which released the album Last Train to Paris before the group ended.

Richard has since built a long independent career outside Bad Boy, making the contrast between those eras central to how she now discusses control and ownership.

The timing also puts the interview beside Richard’s current work. Merge Records released her album Creole Culture on October 9.

The project completes a trilogy she began with New Breed and continued with Second Line, bringing her New Orleans, Haitian and Creole roots to the front.

Richard told The Ebro, Laura, Rosenberg Show in October that New Orleans had been part of her identity from the beginning. “It’s been New Orleans ten toes, like, since I was young,” she said.

She also explained the musical range she wanted on Creole Culture.

“I had no idea if people would receive it, but I wanted to add elements of jazz, Spanish, French, Caribbean, soul, gospel music and pop and try to show people that all of these things represent what we are,” Richard said.

During that October appearance, Richard also traced how she moved from Danity Kane into Diddy-Dirty Money, why she eventually wanted out of Bad Boy and the physical and emotional toll she said the environment took on her.

Her account placed the move toward independence inside a longer process of starting over as an artist and producer.

Her latest remarks come months after a federal judge dismissed 17 of 18 claims in Richard’s civil lawsuit against Combs. Richard had accused the music executive of abuse and exploitation.

Combs denied her allegations, and the June ruling eliminated nearly all of the case on legal grounds.

The new interview is separate from that ruling. It leaves Richard speaking for herself about the culture she says surrounded Diddy-Dirty Money while her present work remains focused on independence and the New Orleans history behind Creole Culture.

item.title: Lil Baby Says Gunna Dispute Will Stay Private For Atlanta’s Sake
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Lil Baby said he and Gunna can keep their dispute off the internet while protecting Atlanta's standing in rap together.
item.content:encoded:
Lil Baby says any problem he has with Gunna will stay off the internet because a public feud would hurt both rappers and the city of Atlanta.

The “Drip Too Hard” collaborators have remained apart since Gunna left jail in December 2022 after entering an Alford plea in the YSL racketeering case. Lil Baby addressed the relationship during an episode of The New York Times’ Popcast, released ahead of his new album, “Fresh.”

He framed the issue as a private matter that should not become a show for fans. Lil Baby said the two men can disagree while staying restrained in public.

“We gonna play it cool for y’all,” he said.

Lil Baby also tied that approach to Atlanta rap’s place in the culture. He argued that an online fight would make the city and its leading artists look divided, no matter who appeared to win.

“I’d rather have that beef or problem personally,” he said.

The comments mark a shift in detail, though not a reunion. Lil Baby did not say the relationship had been repaired or announce new music with Gunna.

He explained how he intends to handle the tension when both artists remain visible representatives of the same city.

Gunna’s Alford plea allowed him to maintain his innocence while accepting a negotiated sentence. He did not testify against Young Thug in the YSL trial, but the plea led to years of snitching accusations and public distance from several artists he had worked with.

Lil Baby and Gunna had built one of Atlanta’s most successful pairings before the split. Their 2018 joint project, “Drip Harder,” included “Drip Too Hard” and turned their chemistry into a defining part of that period in Southern rap.

Lil Baby told AllHipHop in 2024 that the two no longer had a relationship. His latest comments keep that assessment in place while drawing a clear boundary around how he wants to handle any conflict.

The timing also connects the discussion to “Fresh,” released November 6. Lil Baby described the album as a new chapter that pushed him beyond his usual Atlanta production circle.

Its rollout included “Dead Fresh,” a Pharrell Williams-produced single that helped renew his interest in recording.

For now, Lil Baby’s position is clear: the dispute stays personal, and Atlanta is not the stage for it.

item.title: J. Cole’s Dreamville Launches Paris Saint-Germain Collection Online
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: J. Cole's Dreamville launches a Paris Saint-Germain collection with jerseys, hoodies, tees, hats and track pieces.
item.content:encoded:
J. Cole’s Dreamville has turned its partnership with Paris Saint-Germain into a new online merchandise drop, expanding the connection between the rap label and the French soccer club.

The official Dreamville store now carries a full Dreamville x PSG collection. The lineup reaches beyond a simple logo shirt, with jerseys, hoodies, tees, hats, sweatpants, shorts and a track jacket available across the drop.

Prices start at $50 for the satin hat, script hat and Paris beanie. Several tees are listed at $65, while the core hoodie costs $135. The collection also includes an $85 core sweatpant, an $85 pair of nylon shorts and a $135 track jacket.

The soccer-inspired pieces sit at the center of the release. Dreamville’s football jerseys are priced at $110 and come in black, navy and red-stripe designs. The store lists several apparel items in sizes from small through 3XL. It also warns that presale orders will ship in four to six weeks, with tracking sent by text or email.

The release gives fans several ways to wear the collaboration. The lower-priced accessories carry the shared branding, while the jerseys and outerwear build the idea into a complete streetwear line. Buyers can choose a small piece or spend more for one of the main garments.

The collection gives the partnership a wider reach after Dreamville and PSG first teamed up around the 2025 Club World Cup in Los Angeles. That earlier capsule used hoodies and tees to connect the label’s American identity with one of Europe’s most visible soccer brands.

Dreamville is rooted in Hip-Hop, but the PSG link also has a personal connection. J. Cole founded the label, and Dreamville artist Bas was born in Paris and has long shown support for the club. Their roster gives the partnership a natural bridge between music, fashion and soccer.

PSG has built a global streetwear profile through fashion and entertainment collaborations. Dreamville has taken a similar approach with festival merchandise and limited apparel tied to its artists and events. Putting the new line online makes the collaboration available beyond a one-day pop-up or stadium shop.

The current store page does not list an end date for the collection. Availability varies by item and size, and the presale notice means some buyers will wait several weeks before their orders ship.

item.title: Man Arrested For Felony Stalking At LeBron James’ Los Angeles Home
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: A man was arrested for felony stalking at LeBron James' Los Angeles home after police responded to a possible burglary call.
item.content:encoded:
LeBron James‘ Los Angeles home became the scene of a felony stalking arrest Friday night after police answered a call about a possible burglary at the basketball star’s property.

The Los Angeles Police Department confirmed the arrest to KTLA.

Officers responded around 9:40 p.m. on November 6 and took a man into custody at the scene, according to the department’s Media Relations unit.

The station did not identify the suspect or establish whether he had approached James or the property before. LAPD did not provide further details about the circumstances of the arrest.

California’s stalking law covers repeated, malicious following or harassment coupled with a credible threat intended to make someone reasonably fear for their safety or that of an immediate family member.

A credible threat can involve words, electronic communications or a pattern of conduct. The law requires the apparent ability to carry out the threat, while prosecutors do not have to prove the person intended to act on it.

The limited police account did not spell out the conduct behind the stalking allegation or describe a threat.

James was in Cleveland with the Philadelphia 76ers on Friday. His team faced the Cavaliers as part of the NBA Cup, months after he chose Philadelphia over a possible return to his former Cleveland franchise.

He left the Lakers after eight seasons that began in 2018 and included the 2020 NBA title. He chose the 76ers in July, joining Joel Embiid and Tyrese Maxey for his 24th NBA season. His agreement was for two years, with a player option for the second.

James previously dealt with a police investigation at a Los Angeles property in May 2017, when someone painted a racial slur on its front gate on the eve of the NBA Finals.

He was away for that incident too. Officers found that the slur had been covered before they arrived, and investigators sought nearby surveillance footage. That vandalism occurred years before his move to the Lakers.

James was preparing to face the Golden State Warriors with Cleveland when the 2017 vandalism was reported. The incident brought police to a home he had purchased in 2015, before Los Angeles became his NBA base.

item.title: Trap Music Museum Opens New OutKast Exhibit In Atlanta
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Trap Music Museum is opening a new OutKast exhibit in Atlanta celebrating the duo's music, art, fashion and Southern Hip-Hop legacy.
item.content:encoded:
Atlanta’s Trap Music Museum opens a new OutKast exhibit on Monday, November 9, putting one of the city’s most important rap groups at the center of its latest installation.

OutKast, the duo of Andre 3000 and Big Boi, changed the reach of Southern Hip-Hop while keeping Atlanta at the heart of its music.

The new exhibit centers on that impact, with the museum presenting the group as a force across music, art, fashion and the wider culture of the South.

Trap Music Museum general manager Christian “CJ” Johnson discussed the exhibit with FOX 5 Atlanta ahead of the opening. The celebration runs from 8 P.M. to midnight at the museum’s 630 Travis Street NW location.

The free RSVP list filled up before opening night. The museum said a limited number of early registrants will receive email confirmation, while a small batch of general-admission tickets is expected to follow.

The event gives Atlanta fans a chance to see the city’s story told at home. The opening falls on a Monday, outside the museum’s normal Friday-to-Sunday hours. Museum leaders are treating it as a special night, and the exhibit will remain part of the experience after the celebration.

The exhibit arrives as OutKast’s influence continues to move through new generations of Atlanta artists. Andre 3000 and Big Boi released six studio albums as a group, starting with Southernplayalisticadillacmuzik in 1994.

Their 2003 double album Speakerboxxx/The Love Below won the Grammy Award for Album of the Year and pushed the duo deeper into pop culture without cutting their Southern roots.

Trap Music Museum opened in 2018 and has used art, memorabilia and room-sized installations to tell Atlanta rap stories. Its current galleries include work connected to Jeezy, T.I., Rich Homie Quan, Young Thug, Gucci Mane, Future, Migos, 21 Savage and other artists who helped define the city’s sound.

That makes OutKast a natural addition. The duo’s catalog helped turn Atlanta from an underestimated rap market into a global center of Hip-Hop, and its style stretched far beyond records into fashion, film and visual art.

The museum has not released a full list of objects or installations inside the new exhibit. It also has not announced special guests for the opening celebration.

item.title: Mia X Credits Birdman With Securing A “Big Bag” For Verzuz Appearance
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Mia X credited Birdman with making sure she was paid for Verzuz and described her decades-long friendship with Slim.
item.content:encoded:
Mia X credited Birdman with making sure she was properly paid for the Cash Money and No Limit Verzuz battle.

The No Limit veteran shared that account with WZAK’s Sam Sylk while discussing her longstanding ties to Cash Money.

She said she and Cash Money co-founder Slim have been close since 1993 and talk daily. She traced the idea of a feud between the labels largely to their fans.

“Slim is one of my best friends. I speak to him every single day since 1993. Baby made sure that the bag was big for me for Verzuz. We just really have an absolutely great relationship,” Mia X revealed.

Cash Money and No Limit faced off in a Verzuz battle in Las Vegas on October 25, 2025. Mia X represented No Limit during that performance.

Both labels grew out of New Orleans. Master P built No Limit while brothers Birdman and Slim established Cash Money.

Mia X became the first female rapper on No Limit. Her albums included Good Girl Gone Bad in 1995, Unlady Like in 1997 and Mama Drama in 1998. Her No Limit work also included appearances on Master P’s Ice Cream Man and Ghetto D.

Her connection with Master P began in 1994. She recalled working at a record store and performing in New Orleans when C-Murder saw her perform and recommended her to his brother. C-Murder was a regular customer at the store.

This summer, she also outlined plans to release music independently. In July, Mia X announced an album drawing on older unreleased songs and newer recordings.

The plans included collaborations with artists she had long admired and younger women rappers. She said she took charge of the project herself after continuing to write during her time away from the spotlight.

The two label families have since taken their catalogs on the road together with the “Cash Money & No Limit Tour.”

“I can tell you this. Mia X loves Cash Money from the bottom of my heart and the depths of my soul,” the rapper said.

The Cleveland stop is set for November 15 at Rocket Arena, with Mia X among the performers. She said she, Fiend and other acts open the show before the rest of the lineup performs.

Birdman, Master P, Juvenile, Mannie Fresh, B.G., Boosie and Silkk the Shocker are also on the Cleveland bill. The concert is set to begin at 7 p.m.

item.title: Eminem Publisher Demands $41 Million From Suno Over Alleged AI Copying
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Eminem’s publishing dispute bring consent into focus and Elvis Presley representatives challenge synthetic performances.
item.content:encoded:
Eminem’s publisher sued AI music generator Suno in San Francisco federal court seeking approximately $41 million over allegations that the company used his songs without permission.

Eight Mile Style’s complaint puts some of Hip-Hop’s most recognizable compositions at the center of another fight over artificial intelligence. The publisher alleges Suno used copyrighted material to train its technology and enabled users to generate music and lyrics resembling Eminem’s work. Eminem himself is not a plaintiff.

The lawsuit arrived alongside a separate case from Elvis Presley’s rights owners that challenges both the alleged use of copyrighted songs and the reproduction of the singer’s voice. Both cases were brought in the Northern District of California. The accusations remain unproven.

Eight Mile Style controls rights to 269 Eminem compositions. Songs identified in reporting on the complaint include “Lose Yourself,” “Stan” and “The Real Slim Shady.”

The publisher seeks $150,000 for each composition, totaling $40.35 million, plus $672,000 over the alleged removal of copyright information. That brings the requested damages to approximately $41 million. The figure represents what the plaintiffs are pursuing rather than a court award.

The Presley case adds another question to the dispute: whether an AI platform can be held responsible for allowing users to reproduce an identifiable performer’s voice.

Elvis Presley Enterprises and affiliated rights holders allege Suno enabled unauthorized vocal replicas and violated Tennessee’s ELVIS Act. Their complaint also accuses the company of using copyrighted Presley material without permission.

Suno defended its platform in a statement to Billboard.

“Suno exists to help people create new, original music, not to trade on anyone’s name or likeness, and we prohibit any unauthorized use of an artist’s work. To protect against this, we do not allow prompts for specific artists’ names and songs and work with third party providers to screen uploaded audio files and lyrics for potential misuse. We are always working to strengthen our guardrails and we will continue to add new safeguards that protect artists and our users.”

The complaints challenge what happens when technology allegedly draws from that work to produce competing material.

Eight Mile Style seeks compensation for compositions while Presley’s rights owners are also defending his vocal identity. Their claims now await answers in court, where the dispute will turn on evidence rather than how convincingly a machine can deliver a familiar sound.
